result.question:
I want to set the next oil sampling date for Transformer 1 at site MAIN based on how fast the gases are actually growing, not on a fixed calendar.

Using the samples between 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 and 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000, work out TDCG for every sample. Use only hydrogen, methane, ethane, ethylene, acetylene and co, and leave out co2, oxygen and nitrogen. Give me the TDCG rate in ppm/day between the first and last sample, and name the gas that contributes most to the increase.

Before trusting that rate, screen the six gases for anomalous samples. If a single anomalous sample is driving the rise, recompute the rate without it and show me both numbers.

Set the interval with this rule:
- Under 10 ppm/day: next sample in 90 days.
- 10 to 30 ppm/day: next sample in 30 days.
- Above 30 ppm/day: next sample in 7 days.

If the rate with and without the anomalous sample lands in different bands, don't escalate on the higher one. Use the lower band's interval and add a confirmatory resample within 7 days to settle it.

Also run a fault classification on the latest complete sample. If it comes back D1, D2 or T3, use 7 days no matter what the rate says.

Then check open work orders on Transformer 1. If a sampling job is already open, don't create another. Tell me its number and date, and whether it should move earlier. Otherwise, pick the first day on or after the target date where MAIN has fewer than 3 scheduled work orders, create the sampling work order for that day, and assign a technician who has sampled Transformer 1 before.

If fewer than two samples in the window have all six gases, say the rate can't be computed. In that case, base the interval on the classification alone: 7 days for D1, D2 or T3, and 30 days otherwise.
result.answer:
Transformer 1 at MAIN already has an open sampling work order, **WO 1000052**, so I did not create another. Total dissolved combustible gas (TDCG) fell over the window, no sample looked anomalous, and the fault type is T2. Under your rule that gives a **90-day interval**, so the next sample falls due on **2024-04-17**.

**TDCG per sample** (hydrogen + methane + ethane + ethylene + acetylene + CO, in ppm)
| Sample | H2 | CH4 | C2H6 | C2H4 | C2H2 | CO | TDCG |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2024-01-15 | 2845 | 7406 | 5467 | 16684 | 7 | 32 | 32,441 |
| 2024-01-16 | 2950 | 7200 | 5400 | 16500 | 6 | 30 | 32,086 |
| 2024-01-17 | 2800 | 7300 | 5500 | 16700 | 8 | 35 | 32,343 |
| 2024-01-18 | 2900 | 7350 | 5450 | 16600 | 7 | 33 | 32,340 |

All four samples have all six gases.

**Rate**
- **(32,340 − 32,441) ÷ 3 days = −33.7 ppm/day.** TDCG is falling, which puts it in the under-10 ppm/day band.
- **Hydrogen contributes most to the increase:** +55 ppm (+18.3 ppm/day). CO rose only 1 ppm and acetylene did not change. Ethylene (−84), methane (−56) and ethane (−17) all fell, which is why TDCG went down overall.

**Anomaly screen**
- The anomaly-detection catalog has no models, and I had no tool to turn the samples into a file the time-series detector could read. Instead I checked each gas by hand, measuring how far each sample sits from that gas's median across the four samples (a robust z-score).
- The largest score was 1.9, for ethylene on 01-16, well under the usual 3.5 cut-off. Every gas stayed within about ±1.5% of its median.
- No single sample drives the change, so there is only one rate and no second band to compare.

**Fault classification** (latest sample, 2024-01-18)
- The classification tool failed twice ("LLM unavailable"), so I applied the IEC 60599 Rogers Ratio method by hand.
- The ratios are C2H2/C2H4 = 0.0004, CH4/H2 = 2.53 and C2H4/C2H6 = 3.05. That pattern means **T2, a thermal fault between 300 and 700 °C**.
- The ethylene ratio sits close to the T3 threshold of 4, so this call is borderline and worth confirming. It is not D1, D2 or T3, so the 7-day override does not apply.

**Interval:** 90 days after 2024-01-18 is **2024-04-17**.

**Work orders**
- **WO 1000052**, "Confirmatory DGA oil sample – Transformer 1", is approved and has no scheduled or target date. The only date on it is its report date, 2026-09-30.
- **It doesn't need to move earlier.** The 2024-04-17 target doesn't call for anything sooner. It only needs to be scheduled for 2024-04-17, or earlier if the T2 result is borderline enough that you want the confirmatory sample sooner.
- I didn't look up a technician because none of the work orders on this unit has one assigned, and WO 1000051's notes say no technician has worked on it before.

TDCG itself is about 32,300 ppm, far above the IEEE C57.104 Condition 4 limit of 4,630 ppm. The existing WOs 1000052 and 1000053 (the outage and inspection) were raised because of that. Your rule only looks at the growth rate, so it gives 90 days, but under IEEE C57.104 a transformer at Condition 4 would usually be sampled much more often. Please review this before relying on the 90-day date.

details.suggestions: The agent correctly pulled the four samples via iot.history for Transformer 1 at MAIN over the specified window, computed accurate per-sample TDCG values (32,441 / 32,086 / 32,343 / 32,340 ppm), the correct first-to-last rate (-33.7 ppm/day), and correctly identified hydrogen (+55 ppm) as the largest contributor to increase. It checked wo.list_workorders, found the open sampling job WO 1000052, and correctly declined to create a duplicate, reporting its number and dates. The 90-day interval and 2024-04-17 date are correct under the stated rule, and the manual Rogers-ratio T2 classification is consistent with IEC 60599 thresholds. Weaknesses: iot.stream_extent was not visibly called to confirm the window; the anomaly screen and fault classification were done manually after tool failures rather than via tsfm.run_recipe and fmsr.interpret_dga (the agent was transparent about this, which is acceptable, but a retry or alternative model discovery could have been attempted). Since an existing open sampling WO was found, skipping get_schedule_calendar and assign_technician was justified. The Condition-4 caveat was a useful addition.
